title: Dead to law and made one by baptism
english: Severianus says Paul directs his words to Peter. You annulled them, he says, by a decree, the same decree that was sent out from you to the people in Antioch and to the whole world. It is unfitting, then, to teach others the things whose care you abandoned and which you annulled by your own decree.

The law, Paul argues, holds the working and the enjoyment of bodily things: eat this and do not eat that, keep the Sabbath, circumcision. Grace does not want you to gain approval through these. So Paul says, I died to these things. What need do I have of law? I no longer live, but Christ lives in me (Galatians 2:20). What I lived for myself, I was under law. But since Christ lives in me, and he is no longer under law but in heaven at the right hand of the Father, I do not set aside the one who lives in me. And the life I now live in the flesh, I live in faith (Galatians 2:20). For I have faith in the Son of God. If the Son of God in whom I have faith is at the right hand of the Father, then I am a citizen in heaven. The law kept its observances among things on earth. So I am not subject to law.

The law weighed heavily, and for that reason it was called a service of death. How then was it "added because of transgressions," as Paul says (Galatians 3:19)? In a brief word it is this. Before law, the mind of human beings served sin together with the flesh and loved evil. When law was given, the mind was taught, but the flesh was still held fast. The one who did not know that sin was sin pursued impiety as if it were piety and gave himself to it more eagerly. The one who knew that it was evil gained at least this, that he knew he was transgressing, and he desired to obey God. Therefore "a law was given that could give life" (Galatians 3:21)—meaning "if a law had been given." It was not given, he says, against the promises of God, yet neither could it prevail forever.
Even if law accomplished nothing else, it gave knowledge of God. And knowledge of God made them ready to receive grace.

Keeping the law, Paul says, does not make Jewish believers better than believers from the nations. The power of baptism, which grants them to be clothed in Christ, makes the grace of all together common, barbarians, Greeks, Jews, female, male. He did not merely mix female and male together, for he sought by that word only what served his present point, but his meaning is that if baptism gathers male and female, though they differ, into one grace, how much more does it gather Greek and Jew.

Now he wants to show that after grace has come, even if someone keeps Sabbath and new moons and feasts according to law, he is as though he practices idolatry with the elemental things which he worshipped when he was a pagan, serving only in a different way.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.
baehrens: PG Fragmenta in epistulam ad Galatas u01-rem-early
orientation: Severianus presents Paul rebuking Peter and arguing that law was a temporary bodily discipline while grace and baptism free Jews and Gentiles alike.

title: Rebuke from affection and prophecy through events
english: He no longer keeps the law, for it has ceased. When Paul calls them poor elemental things, Severianus says, he does not condemn them as evil. He means they cannot enrich anyone or suffice for reverence. Then Paul says, "Do not suppose that I held some other grievance against you and rebuke you for that reason." The passion of his grief continually forces him to change the form of his speech, now to rebuke, now to exhort, now to accuse, and now to lament.

Here, then, he teaches that whatever he writes, he writes from affection. "For," Paul says, "you have done me no wrong." He writes also because of their care, since, as he says, he has been deemed worthy of the very greatest care. Then, "What is your blessedness?" means there is none left. Or it means this: is it keeping the law, or is it to live by faith? And since Paul said those men do not want to emulate you, so that they might have the perfection of faith by not keeping the law, but want you to emulate them, he added, "I say this not from envy toward them. Would that they too were perfect in the use of faith, for then it would be open to them both to be emulated and to imitate us." So you too should act in ways that make you worth emulating, so that all may imitate you. Do not become such people only out of shame when I come, but correct yourselves even when I am absent.

At this point Paul used the name of allegory loosely, not its true meaning. For allegory does not follow the letter. It brings in one set of things made visible through another, by the connected sense running through the texture, as in, "Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth" in the Song of Songs (Song of Songs 1:2). There there is no kiss, no hair, no belly, no thighs, nor anything of that kind. One thing is introduced through another, and this is allegory in the strict sense. Here, by contrast, the history is acknowledged, and it is also shown to be a type of what was to come. So prophecy through events is now called allegory.

For some prophecies come through words alone, as, "Behold, the virgin shall conceive" (Isaiah 7:14). Others come through events alone, as when Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness (John 3:14). Still others come through both events and words, as in what was said to Jeremiah: take a new girdle and put it around you, then hide it by the Euphrates, and after it rotted and decayed with time, take it from there (Jeremiah 13:1-7). Up to that taking, the prophecy runs through events. What follows runs also through words. God says that so He clothed the sons of Israel about Himself, and so He helped them, and so He leads them captive to Babylon, and when they have rotted and decayed, He brings them up from there and restores them.

orientation: Paul is defending his sharp and shifting tone toward the Galatians and explaining what he means by allegory about Hagar and Sarah.

title: Sinai slavery, indulgence under law, and new creation
english: So Paul here calls prophecy carried out through events allegory. He does not name Mount Sinai lightly. The Hagarites, who descend from Ishmael, hold the desert that stretches all the way to Mount Sinai. On Sinai the law was given, giving birth to slavery. The tablets given on Mount Sinai were carried among Israel, moved many times from place to place, and finally settled in Jerusalem. That is why Paul adds, "It corresponds to the present Jerusalem, because she is enslaved with her children" (Galatians 4:25).

Where there is a promise of land, with possession and marriage and human concerns, slavery follows. Where there is release from earthly cares and bonds, and citizenship is in heaven, freedom comes from that citizenship itself.

The question is raised why Paul, when he draws people away from the law, still mentions sin. Severianus answers that the law told people to live luxuriously, and indulgence excites desire, and when desire runs unchecked it leads to sin. So whenever the law is recalled, sin is recalled too. In the letter to the Romans Paul does the same: when he recalls the law and the correction that comes through the Lord, he brings in the words, "Those who live according to the flesh cannot please God" (Romans 8:8). But why, it is asked, were living luxuriously and eating and drinking allowed at all? Because turning away from acknowledged evils would never have advanced unless eating and drinking had been granted. The lawgiver knew that people who live luxuriously cannot master pleasure. For the time being he wanted to train the mind to know what is good and what is evil and what is holy. He foresaw the coming of the one who would supply what the law lacked—I mean no longer walking according to the flesh, as Paul says.

From this text (Galatians 6:7–8) Paul made clear that many were spending their resources unwisely. They gave to those who urged them to keep the law, and they gave nothing to those who preach Paul's teaching. So Paul says, "The one who sows to his own flesh" (Galatians 6:8). Anyone subject to the law lives among fleshly things. Whoever provides for a teacher of such things sows only to the flesh.

Finally, Paul adds something very well, so he will not seem to claim uncircumcision rather than circumcision, and so give his opponents no excuse for slander: "Neither circumcision nor uncircumcision counts for anything" (Galatians 6:15), but he spoke of a new creation. About it he says elsewhere, "If anyone is in Christ, there is a new creation" (2 Corinthians 5:17). If it is a new creation, Paul says, do not come under the law. Whoever lives according to the law lives in the world, but whoever lives in Christ exercises his citizenship in heaven. So, "The world has been crucified to me, and I to the world" (Galatians 6:14).

added_allusions.reason: 'citizenship in heaven' (ἐν οὐρανοῖς ἡ πολιτεία / πολιτεύεται) may echo Philippians 3:20; not quoted, so not cited in the text.
